study_identification_part.si4_title: Replicating extensive brain structural heterogeneity in individuals with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: This study aimed to replicate previous findings of substantial interindividual heterogeneity in brain structural aberrations among patients with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Using normative modeling with Gaussian process regression on voxel-based morphometry data, the authors sought to map individual deviations from healthy ranges in two independent replication samples.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni-Holm correction for multiple comparisons were used to test associations between diagnosis and percentage of extreme deviations. Correlation analyses (Pearson r) were performed to assess associations between extreme deviations and PANSS symptom scores, age of disorder onset, and other clinical characteristics. Permutation-based inference using PALM was employed to test for mean group differences in Z-scores between healthy individuals, patients with schizophrenia, and patients with bipolar disorder.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: The study successfully replicated substantial interindividual heterogeneity in brain structural aberrations in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder; while robust group-level differences were found between patients and healthy individuals, only a small proportion of patients showed extreme deviations from normality in the same brain regions.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Across three independent samples (discovery and two replications), patients with schizophrenia showed significantly higher percentages of extreme negative deviations (0.64-1.09% of voxels) compared to healthy individuals (0.16-0.22%) and patients with bipolar disorder (0.14-0.35%). Extreme negative deviations were 3.91, 4.00, and 4.95 times more prevalent in schizophrenia patients than healthy controls across the three samples. Peak voxel overlap for extreme negative deviations was sparse: 9.57% and 9.52% for schizophrenia, 5.17% and 8.19% for bipolar disorder in the two replication samples. Extreme negative deviations correlated significantly with PANSS total scores across all samples (r=0.157-0.241, p<0.05) and with age of disorder onset for both conditions. Group-level differences showed robust mean negative deviations in frontal, temporal, and cerebellar regions for schizophrenia, with bipolar disorder showing weaker replication (cerebellum differences only in discovery sample). The findings confirm that robust group effects translate to relatively sparse overlap of extreme deviations at the individual level.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study emphasizes that moving beyond group-level analyses to individual-level characterization is essential for understanding variability within clinical cohorts. The authors provide publicly available analytical pipelines to facilitate replication by independent researchers. They note that while structural MRI shows substantial heterogeneity, other modalities or network-level analyses may reveal different patterns. The findings have important implications for the interpretation and generalization of group-level brain imaging findings to individual patients with mental disorders, supporting the need for personalized approaches in psychiatric neuroimaging.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: The study was conducted primarily on adult samples, while schizophrenia onset typically occurs in adolescence or early adulthood, limiting generalizability to younger age groups. Sample sizes for bipolar disorder and schizophrenia groups were smaller in the replication samples compared to the discovery sample, which may have contributed to weaker replication of some findings (e.g., cerebellar differences in bipolar disorder). The study did not implement multi-site harmonization methods, analyzing each scanner acquisition separately; the authors acknowledge ongoing work to improve normative modeling across sites. Other data modalities beyond structural MRI (e.g., functional connectivity, network-level measures) may show different patterns of heterogeneity. The correlation between extreme deviations and PANSS scores was significant only when pooling bipolar and schizophrenia groups, not within individual diagnostic groups, suggesting the effect may be driven by group differences rather than true dimensional relationships. The study used a predominantly Scandinavian population from a single catchment area, which may limit generalizability to other populations.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a direct replication study of Wolfers et al. 2018 (JAMA Psychiatry) using identical analytical procedures. The study used three independent samples from the same population (TOP study) but acquired on different scanners: Discovery (1.5T Siemens Sonata, n_HC=256, n_SZ=163, n_BP=190), Replication 1 (3T GE 750 Discovery, n_HC=400, n_SZ=94, n_BP=116), and Replication 2 (3T GE Signa HDxT with two different coils, n_HC=312, n_SZ=105, n_BP=61). All samples were selected from the NoDa (local NORMENT database) on September 25, 2019, with no overlap between discovery and replication samples. The study found that sex stratification increased overlap of extreme deviations, with overlap driven by males across studies (Supplementary Figure 9). Multiple thresholds were tested for robustness (|Z|>1.96, |Z|>2.6, |Z|>3.1, FDR=0.05, and extreme value distribution), all showing consistent patterns of heterogeneity. The analytical code is publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/RindKind/). Diagnostic assessments used SCID (Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV Axis I Disorders) and PANSS for symptom assessment.
